analysis.one_liner: Imposed a four-month freeze on lawsuits to collect Puerto Rico's government debt.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced December 18, 2015 with 4 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee until the 114th Congress ended with no action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill from Senator Elizabeth Warren would have frozen all lawsuits, liens, and collection actions against Puerto Rico's government until April 1, 2016 — the same kind of automatic "stay" a bankruptcy filing creates — with narrow exceptions where a court found cause. The point was to stop creditors from draining the island's dwindling cash while Congress worked out a comprehensive debt solution for a territory of 3.5 million U.S. citizens that could not file for bankruptcy. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Puerto Rico's 3.5 million residents, whose government was running out of cash to pay for public safety, health care, and education. By blocking collection suits and liens for roughly 15 weeks, the bill would have kept tax dollars and utility revenue flowing to services instead of to creditors, and given Congress time to design a lasting fix — the bill's stated purpose (Sections 2 and 6).

how_it_helps.text: Would have automatically halted every lawsuit, judgment enforcement, lien, and collection action against Puerto Rico's government and its agencies and public corporations until April 1, 2016, with court-ordered relief available only in limited cases.

Would have protected essential public services — public safety, health care, and education — from a 'disorderly race to the courthouse' by creditors as the government's cash ran short, according to the bill's own findings.

Would have bought Congress time to write a comprehensive debt-relief plan, since Puerto Rico's debt spanned 18 different issuers and many creditor groups with conflicting interests, making any negotiated resolution difficult without federal action.

analysis.who_pays: Holders of Puerto Rico government bonds and loans — hedge funds, mutual funds, bond insurers, and individual municipal-bond investors — who would have been barred for nearly four months from suing, enforcing liens, foreclosing on collateral, or offsetting debts, with court relief only for cause or to prevent irreparable damage to their property interests.

drawbacks.text: The bill fixed nothing by itself. The stay expired April 1, 2016, so unless Congress enacted a comprehensive restructuring plan in the meantime, creditors could simply resume collection with the underlying crisis unresolved — the bill's stated purpose was only to 'provide a limited period of time.'
The freeze was uneven: lawsuits and proceedings already filed before enactment were exempt from the stay, so creditors who had moved fastest kept their claims moving while others were held back.

Creditors had a fair argument that blocking collection without any repayment framework left their investments in limbo and risked making it harder for Puerto Rico to borrow at affordable rates in the future — a cost that would ultimately fall on the island's own residents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade was real but temporary: a 15-week shield for services serving 3.5 million U.S. citizens in exchange for a four-month delay for bondholders, with court escape valves for parties who could show cause or irreparable harm. The bigger weakness was design — it bought time rather than resolving anything, and it carved out lawsuits already filed. Still, as an emergency measure during an acute cash crisis, the costs fell on sophisticated creditors while the benefits went to ordinary residents of the island.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on December 18, 2015, and the committee never held a hearing or vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on December 18, 2015 with Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid and Senators Blumenthal and Schumer as original cosponsors, framing it as an emergency response to Puerto Rico's fiscal and liquidity crisis.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day — the only action ever taken on it.
The committee, chaired by Republican Lisa Murkowski, took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Puerto Rico's creditors came out ahead: they remained free to sue and press collection claims with no stay in place. Puerto Rico's 3.5 million residents got no breathing room, and the comprehensive federal solution the bill was meant to make room for never came from this Congress.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a temporary automatic stay on collection actions against Puerto Rico's government.

for.name: 4 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators signed on.

against.name: Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in her committee from referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never advanced beyond committee.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill and the Republican-controlled agenda never allowed it a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were Democrats, out of 44 Senate Democrats; no Republican ever cosponsored, no vote was ever held, and a Republican chair and Republican majority kept it from advancing.

industries.industry: Puerto Rico government bondholders (hedge funds, mutual funds, insurers, individual muni investors)
industries.note: The bill would have frozen their lawsuits, liens, and collection efforts against Puerto Rico's government until April 1, 2016, delaying repayment of the island's debts. In this bill, what creditors stood to gain — faster access to the government's shrinking cash — is exactly what the island's residents stood to lose in services, so their interest ran against the public's.

industries.industry: Municipal bond and distressed-debt investment funds specializing in Puerto Rico paper
industries.note: Funds built around Puerto Rico's government debt would have faced a stay on enforcement, including against pledged property such as agency revenue, for the duration of the freeze, with relief only where a court found their collateral unprotected or the property nonessential.
